items.title: Ran Blake interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 16, 2021
items.q: thank gosh I’ve had Gunther Schuller to start me off... These are faculty

ctx.x: talked about in a recent interview with Ornette Coleman, and Ornette sitting in with the Herb Pomeroy Orchestra and you had this wonderful analogy, I believe it was yours, that it was like mixing water from the bayou with water from the North Pole.

I like the water from the bayou, I swim. I believe I said that, that was at the Music in the Berkshires. And I love Herb. I know Fred Harris from MIT is doing a biography, and I love his appreciation of Duke, the sound of the orchestra. But when you think that Phil Woods is going to play and suddenly pops out Ornette, it was explosive. John Lewis went like that, Martin Williams, a wonderful critic, really practically flipped, and of course Gunther was sitting there — this was an afternoon rehearsal but Gunther…

Well what brought me to this was Karl Berger was led to this statement. He had heard Eric Dolphy in ’64 and we were talking about freedom and free jazz. And he said, “More freedom is not about less precision, it’s about more precision. The more precise you get the more free you are.” He says, “I’m creating my own rules and they’re much more stringent.” I wonder if you could comment on that, because it’s always fascinated me, we think about free jazz as the ultimate no constraints, and he’s saying the opposite.

items.title: Schuller Gunther — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I brought him to Boston, and eventually I was able to create that... developed a Third Stream department there with people like Ran Blake

ctx.x: Yeah, and I just said, this is what we’re going to do. It took me about a year to actually create the department, because I had to hire jazz players who were going to be on the faculty. I had to get students and all of that. But that’s the first thing that I did, because I said to myself, here is 1967. Jazz has been around since – in some form or another since, let’s say, 1900 or 1910, whatever date you want to give the beginnings of it. Here we are. This is one of the great and oldest conservatories in the…

else is imported from Europe, even the popular musics of the 19th century, the Irish jigs and all the dance music. That all came from Scotland and Ireland and so on. So here’s jazz, created by black people, and it is the music that is completely ignored in the educational system. There were – a university in Texas and Indiana University had a – they – I shouldn’t say they had. There was a jazz orchestra there. By the way, that was created by David Baker, who was a student at Indiana University. But Dean Bain, the…
